name: Striped bass
marks: Long, dark horizontal stripes
Two distinct dorsal fins
Silvery sides and a powerful forked tail
habitat: An estuary and coastal fish that moves between salt and fresh water. Occurrence is seasonal; a map pin is not a catch forecast.
tackle: A medium saltwater spinning setup and a small swimming lure suit shore exploration. Non-offset circle hooks are required when fishing for striped bass with bait; check DEC details.

name: Bluefish
marks: Blue-green back, silver sides
Large mouth with sharp teeth
Deeply forked tail
habitat: A schooling coastal predator. Young bluefish are often called snappers.
tackle: Use pliers and a bite-resistant leader. A casting spoon imitates small baitfish; match it to your rod rating. Keep fingers clear of the mouth.

name: Summer flounder
marks: Both eyes usually on the left side
Flattened, mottled body
Several eye-like spots on the upper side
habitat: Also called fluke. Often found on sandy or muddy coastal bottoms. Winter flounder is a different species.
tackle: A light bucktail or bait rig can work near the bottom. Use only enough weight to maintain contact and follow current size and season rules.

name: Scup
marks: Deep, compressed silver body
Small mouth and relatively small head
Long spiny dorsal fin
habitat: Also called porgy. A coastal bottom-feeding species associated with structure.
tackle: Small baited hooks and a simple bottom rig help present a small offering. A non-lead sinker reduces unnecessary lead use.

name: Black sea bass
marks: Dark body with pale scale centers
Long continuous dorsal fin
Larger males can have a raised forehead
habitat: A coastal fish associated with reefs, wrecks and other structure. Color changes with age and sex.
tackle: Use a small bait rig around structure with a leader suitable for abrasion. Check current seasons; they change during the year.

name: Largemouth bass
marks: Upper jaw extends behind the eye
Dark horizontal band along the side
Notch between spiny and soft dorsal fins
habitat: A warmwater predator found around vegetation, cover and lake edges.
tackle: A weedless soft lure helps around aquatic plants. Use barbless hooks and non-lead weights in NYC park waters.

name: Bluegill
marks: Dark flap at the rear of the gill cover
Deep oval body
Dark patch near the rear of the dorsal fin
habitat: A small sunfish often found near vegetation and shoreline cover.
tackle: A small barbless hook, a float and a short piece of worm provide a simple starting rig. Keep hooks small for the small mouth.

name: Pumpkinseed
marks: Orange-red spot at the edge of the dark ear flap
Wavy blue-green lines on the cheek
Speckled, deep-bodied sides
habitat: A colorful sunfish in quiet, vegetated fresh water. Juveniles and hybrids can be hard to separate from other sunfish.
tackle: Use a small barbless hook and float, as for bluegill. Check the cheek and ear flap before choosing a species.

name: Black crappie
marks: Irregular dark mottling over silver sides
Deep body and large mouth
Usually seven or eight dorsal spines
habitat: A freshwater fish often associated with submerged cover. White crappie can look similar.
tackle: A tiny jig or small bait beneath a float is useful around cover. Cast gently and keep the hook barbless.

name: Yellow perch
marks: Dark vertical bars on yellow-green sides
Two separate dorsal fins
Orange or yellow lower fins
habitat: A schooling freshwater fish. Young fish may show paler colors than adults.
tackle: A small jig or a baited barbless hook beneath a float keeps the setup simple. Do not infer current abundance from historical survey records.

name: Common carp
marks: Two pairs of barbels near the mouth
Large scales and a long dorsal fin
Thick body with a downward-facing mouth
habitat: An introduced freshwater fish. It can grow large in city lakes; goldfish generally lack its mouth barbels.
tackle: A sturdy spinning rod and a simple bottom presentation are practical. Use a soft landing net and keep a large fish supported.

name: Brown bullhead
marks: Whisker-like barbels around the mouth
Mottled brown body without scales
Tail squared or slightly rounded
habitat: A freshwater catfish found in several NYC park lakes. Other catfish can be difficult to separate from a single photograph.
tackle: A small bottom rig and pliers are helpful. Avoid the sharp fin spines; identify the fish in the water when possible.
